198196.intro: A one-hour concert under the arcades of the Galleria Principe di Napoli, between the Academy of Fine Arts and the Archaeological Museum. The classic Neapolitan repertoire is played and sung with no microphones and no amplification: just voices and instruments, the way it was done in drawing rooms and at parties long ago. The performers change every night, so no two shows are the same. With almost seven hundred reviews averaging 4.9, it's the most booked show of all the ones we list.
cosaSiFa: You arrive at the meeting point, under the Galleria's arcades, fifteen minutes early: that's for check-in and for settling into the room. It's an intimate space and the chairs are all on one level, so whoever arrives first gets the best seats. A drink is served before the start, included in the ticket.

Then the concert proper begins. Musicians and singers, sometimes actors and dancers too, work through the best-known Neapolitan songs, the ones everyone has heard at least once even without knowing the title. No microphones: the voice reaches you directly, with all its shading and every breath, and in a room this small you catch every detail.

The finale is always the same, and it's the part people remember most: it ends with 'O sole mio sung by everyone, audience included. After exactly one hour you're back out in the Galleria, a couple of minutes from Piazza Museo and Piazza Dante, with the evening still ahead of you.
198196.perChi: Good if you have a free evening after dinner and want something Neapolitan without committing to a long night: one hour, then you're back on the street. It works for couples, solo travellers and anyone bringing their parents. If you're after a big theatre with a raised stage and a guaranteed view, you'll be disappointed: the room is small, and the closeness is the whole point.
198196.consiglio: Get there well before the requested fifteen minutes: the room is small and the front seats go fast. Before the concert, take a look round the Archaeological Museum right next door, or head to Piazza Bellini for an aperitivo; afterwards, the old town is five minutes' walk away. Book a few days ahead, it often sells out.

faq.q: How long is the concert and where is it held?
faq.a: It lasts one hour. The meeting point is in Piazza Museo, under the arcades of the Galleria Principe di Napoli, between the Academy of Fine Arts and the National Archaeological Museum. You need to be there fifteen minutes before your booked time. Start times vary by date and are shown when you book.

faq.q: What's included in the ticket?
faq.a: The one-hour concert and a drink served in the room. The performers sing and play without microphones or amplification, and the evening ends with 'O sole mio sung together with the audience. You don't need anything else: turn up, sit down and listen.

faq.q: Can I cancel if my plans change?
faq.a: Yes, cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the start, with a full refund. You can also book now and pay later. Bear in mind that dates often sell out, so it's worth securing your seat as soon as you're sure of the evening.

209424P1.intro: Capri seen first from the sea and then from land, on the same day. You start with an hour in a gozzo, the island's traditional wooden boat, past caves and coves all along the coast. Then a minibus climbs to Anacapri, where you get a couple of hours for the village, the chairlift up Monte Solaro or lunch. You finish in Capri town, with the Piazzetta, the lanes of designer boutiques and the Giardini di Augusto looking out over the Faraglioni rocks.
cosaSiFa: You meet in the morning at the port of Naples, at Molo Beverello, or mid-morning directly at Marina Grande if you're already on the island. First up is the boat: a full one-hour loop around Capri in a gozzo, with the caves, the coves and the Faraglioni seen from the water. It's the part that stays with you longest.

Once ashore, a minibus takes you up to Anacapri, the upper part of the island. You have about two hours here: the village is easy to explore on foot, and you can take the chairlift up Monte Solaro (extra cost) or stop for something to eat. Then it's down to Capri town: the Piazzetta, the boutique-lined lanes and the Giardini di Augusto, the terrace with the best view of the Faraglioni.
209424P1.perChi: For anyone who wants it all in one go: sea, Anacapri and Capri town, without piecing it together themselves. The guide speaks English, Spanish and Italian. It's wheelchair accessible and suitable for all fitness levels, and pushchairs are allowed. Groups are up to twenty people. If you get seasick, think carefully about the hour on the boat.
209424P1.consiglio: Bring sunglasses, sun cream and a hat: there's no shade on a gozzo for an hour. Wear walking shoes, as there are plenty of steps between Anacapri and Capri's lanes. If you book the option starting from Capri, you buy your own ferry ticket. Lunch isn't included: Anacapri, with its two hours, is the place to eat.

faq.q: Where do we meet and how long does it last?
faq.a: At the port of Naples, Molo Beverello, at 8:30am; or at Marina Grande on the island at 10:30am if you choose the option from Capri. The day lasts between eight and nine hours, including the return.

faq.q: What does the price include?
faq.a: The one-hour boat tour, the minibus on the island, the guide in English, Spanish and Italian, the visit to Anacapri and Capri, and entry to the Giardini di Augusto. It doesn't include lunch, the Monte Solaro chairlift or tips. The ferry isn't included in the option from Capri.

faq.q: Is it suitable for children and people with limited mobility? Can I cancel?
faq.a: Yes: it's listed as wheelchair accessible and suitable for all fitness levels, with prams and pushchairs allowed. Infants travel on an adult's lap. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before departure.

220821.intro: The two cities buried by Vesuvius in AD 79, seen on the same day with an archaeologist guide and a group of no more than twenty. Pompeii in the morning, then the Circumvesuviana train (the local railway round Vesuvius) and Herculaneum in the afternoon: smaller but better preserved, with the upper floors of its houses still standing. People with just one day for the Vesuvian sites usually pick one of the two: here you see both, with tickets already in hand.
cosaSiFa: You meet in Piazza Esedra, in front of the Pompeii entrance, with ID in your pocket. The guide already has the tickets, so you skip the ticket-office queue. The visit lasts two hours and follows the streets of the Roman city: houses, shops and public spaces, explained by someone who does archaeology for a living. If the group is larger than ten, headsets are handed out.

After Pompeii there's a half-hour break, just enough for a sandwich or a look round the shops outside the ruins: lunch isn't included and there's no time to waste. Then you take the Circumvesuviana to Herculaneum together, a ride of about twenty minutes, with the one-way ticket already included in the price.

At Herculaneum you set off on another two-hour guided visit. Here the blanket of mud sealed in charred wood, frescoes and mosaics that didn't survive at Pompeii. The tour ends at the Herculaneum Archaeological Park, with no organised return: from there you make your own way back to Naples or Pompeii by public transport.
220821.perChi: For anyone who wants to really understand the difference between the two cities, not just see them, and who appreciates a small group with a well-prepared guide. The pace is brisk and there's a lot of walking on uneven Roman paving: not suitable for anyone with mobility issues or using a wheelchair, nor for anyone after a relaxed day.
220821.consiglio: In summer bring a hat, sunglasses and a bottle of water: there's little shade at either site. For the half-hour break it's best to have something to eat with you already. If you're staying in Naples, get to Piazza Esedra on the Circumvesuviana, getting off at Pompei Scavi.

faq.q: How long does it last and where does it end?
faq.a: About five and a half hours in total: two hours at Pompeii, a half-hour break, the train to Herculaneum and another two hours of visiting. It ends at the exit of the Herculaneum Archaeological Park, not at the starting point.

faq.q: What's included in the price?
faq.a: The archaeologist guide for the whole day, the entry tickets to Pompeii and Herculaneum, and the one-way Circumvesuviana ticket between the two sites. Meals, drinks and transport to Pompeii or back from Herculaneum aren't included.

faq.q: What language is it in, and can I cancel?
faq.a: The tour is available in Italian and English, depending on the date you choose. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the start, with a full refund. Remember to bring your passport or ID card.

23258P122.intro: Two hours in the Herculaneum ruins with an archaeologist, in a group of no more than fifteen, with ticket and earpieces included. Herculaneum is smaller than Pompeii but better preserved: the eruption of AD 79 covered it with a layer that kept the air out, so the charred wood of beams and furniture survived, along with mosaics and paintings whose colours are almost intact. It was a town of merchants and nobles, and it shows.
cosaSiFa: You meet at the ruins and go in with the ticket already bought by the operator. With the earpieces you can hear the archaeologist even when you drift a little away from the group. You start at the ancient shoreline: the remains of more than three hundred people who were waiting to escape by sea were found along the waterfront, and it's the hardest moment of the visit.

Then you climb up into the streets of the town. The planned stops are the Samnite House, the baths, the Temple of the Augustales, the forum, the House of Neptune and Amphitrite with its mosaic, the gymnasium and the House of the Wooden Partition. The archaeologist explains what you're looking at and what sets Herculaneum apart from Pompeii, starting with the charred wood and the colours of the paintings.

Two hours isn't enough to cover the whole site: the visit is a considered selection, with time for questions, which is the real advantage of a group of fifteen. The pace is relaxed and you stop for a good while in front of the best-preserved mosaics and frescoes.
23258P122.perChi: Ideal if you have half a day and want to really understand what you're looking at: the archaeologist makes all the difference compared with going on your own. The small group also helps with teenagers. You walk for two hours outdoors on ancient streets, so you need proper shoes. If you want to see the whole site at leisure, add some time after the tour.
23258P122.consiglio: You reach Herculaneum from Naples on the Circumvesuviana, getting off at Ercolano Scavi, and the two-hour tour leaves the afternoon free to add Vesuvius, just a few kilometres away. In summer pick the morning slot: there's little shade inside. Hat, water and closed shoes.

faq.q: Is the entry ticket included?
faq.a: Yes. The price includes entry to the Herculaneum ruins, the two-hour guided visit with an archaeologist, and earpieces so you can follow the explanation even from a distance. The group is limited to fifteen people.

faq.q: What languages is the tour in?
faq.a: The tour is available in Italian, English, German, Spanish and French. You choose the language when you book and the group is formed accordingly, always with an archaeologist as guide.

faq.q: How long does it last and how do I cancel?
faq.a: About two hours, all inside the ruins, starting from the site entrance. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the tour's start time.

276598P12.intro: Forty-five minutes in the Sansevero Chapel with a licensed guide, ticket included. The star is the Veiled Christ, the marble statue whose veil looks like fabric; around it are the other Baroque statues commissioned by Raimondo di Sangro, the prince who had the whole place built, and in the crypt the two Anatomical Machines, skeletons with their circulatory systems reconstructed. Without an explanation you see a chapel; with the guide you understand what lies behind it.
cosaSiFa: You meet in Piazza San Domenico Maggiore, with the guide at the chapel entrance, a few steps from the square. You go in with the ticket already bought, and the guide starts with the story of Prince Raimondo di Sangro, who commissioned the chapel, and the esoteric symbols hidden among the Baroque sculptures.

Then you stop in front of the Veiled Christ: the guide explains how it was carved and tells the legends that grew up around the marble veil. You go round the other sculptures and finally head down into the crypt, home to the Anatomical Machines. Forty-five minutes in all, with a group of no more than twenty.
276598P12.perChi: Good if you're short on time and want the most famous thing in the old town with a proper explanation, without worrying about tickets. Fine for families with children who can manage 45 minutes of listening. If you'd rather look in silence, without a group, you can buy a standard ticket; here the value is the guide.
276598P12.consiglio: After the chapel you're in the heart of Spaccanapoli: San Domenico Maggiore, the Nile statue and Via San Gregorio Armeno are a few minutes' walk away. Book ahead, especially at weekends and on Italian bank holidays, because the chapel is small and time slots sell out fast.

faq.q: Is the ticket included?
faq.a: Yes, the entry ticket to the Sansevero Chapel is included, along with the visit with a licensed guide. The visit also includes going down into the crypt with the Anatomical Machines, as well as the Veiled Christ and the other sculptures.

faq.q: How long does it last and where do we meet?
faq.a: About 45 minutes. The meeting point is Piazza San Domenico Maggiore, with the guide waiting at the chapel entrance. Groups are no more than twenty people.

faq.q: What languages is it in, and can I cancel?
faq.a: The tour is in Italian, English or French, chosen when you book. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the start of the visit.

297875P1.intro: Two hours in a pizzeria on Via San Carlo, opposite the opera house, with an English-speaking pizzaiolo who gets your hands in the dough. It's not a demonstration: you make the dough yourself, starting from the flour, then slice the mozzarella and prepare the tomato. You eat what you've made, with bruschetta first and tiramisù after, drink included. Groups of up to fifteen.
cosaSiFa: The first part is theory and practice on the dough: the pizzaiolo explains the ingredients and the technique, then everyone kneads their own dough ball following his lead. Meanwhile the bruschetta arrives. Then on to the toppings: you slice the mozzarella and make the tomato sauce with fresh ingredients supplied by the pizzeria.

Next you stretch your pizza, it goes in the oven and you eat it in the pizzeria with a drink. The tiramisù, which shares top billing with the pizza, rounds off the meal. Two hours in all, in English. At the end you walk out onto Via San Carlo, with the theatre in front of you and Piazza del Plebiscito just round the corner.
297875P1.perChi: Good if you speak English and want to learn dough from a real pizzaiolo, in a working pizzeria rather than a teaching kitchen. Suits couples, friends and families; two hours is manageable with children too. If you can't follow English, you'll miss the explanations. The location, opposite the San Carlo, makes it easy to fit into a day in the centre.
297875P1.consiglio: Don't have lunch beforehand: bruschetta, pizza and tiramisù are plenty. The class is opposite Teatro San Carlo and a step from Galleria Umberto I and Piazza del Plebiscito: arrive a little early and have a wander. Wear clothes that can take some flour, and come with clean hands.

faq.q: What's included?
faq.a: A theory and hands-on class with an English-speaking pizzaiolo, fresh ingredients and equipment, bruschetta, the pizza you've made, tiramisù and a drink. You eat everything in the pizzeria, so it counts as a full meal.

faq.q: How long does it last and where is it held?
faq.a: About two hours, in a pizzeria on Via San Carlo in central Naples, opposite the theatre. Groups are no more than fifteen people. The exact address comes with your booking confirmation.

faq.q: What language is it in, and can I cancel?
faq.a: The class is in English, with an English-speaking pizzaiolo. You can cancel free of charge up to 24 hours before the class starts.

299918P1.intro: Two hours on a farm in Massa Lubrense, at the tip of the Sorrento peninsula, to see where the Sorrento lemon comes from before it ends up in a bottle. You see the seedbed, the field of mother plants and a graft made right in front of you, walk under the traditional pergola and climb to a viewpoint looking out to Ischia, Procida and the Bay of Naples. Along the way you taste what the farm produces: lemonade, limoncello, cream of limoncello, orange and cinnamon liqueur, jams and olive oil. The meeting point is the bus stop in the main square of Massa Lubrense, with departures at 10am and 5pm.
cosaSiFa: The guide meets you at the EAV and SITA bus stop in the village square and walks you to the farm. You start sitting down, with a glass of lemonade and lemon slices with sugar, which is how they're eaten round here, peel and all. Then into the seedbed: this is where bitter orange seeds are planted, because the Sorrento lemon doesn't grow on its own roots but on those of a sturdier plant.

From the seedbed you move on to the field of mother plants, the mature trees from which the cutting for the graft is taken. The next stop is the viewpoint: from there you can see Ischia, Procida, the whole Bay of Naples and the centre of Massa Lubrense. You stop for photos and the first round of tastings, limoncello, cream of limoncello and orange and cinnamon liqueur, while the guide tells how the lemon reached this coast.

After the break comes the part almost nobody has ever seen: grafting. The guide shows how the rootstock is cut, how the cutting is inserted and how it's tied, then shows you young plants already grafted, at various stages of growth. It's the moment you understand why a lemon grove takes years before it bears fruit.

The way back runs under the Sorrento pergola, the structure of chestnut poles and netting that shields the lemons from wind and cold and turns these plots into green corridors. You finish back at the start with lemon and ginger jam and orange and cinnamon jam, a drizzle of olive oil and a few minutes to sit down before heading back to the square.
299918P1.perChi: For anyone on holiday in Sorrento or on the peninsula who wants a slow half-day away from the crowded main street, and for families: there's little walking, on easy ground, pushchairs can get through and children from two up have their own rate. It also works if you know nothing about farming, because the guide starts from the basics. Less suited to anyone after a proper walk or trail scenery: you stay on the farm, and the point is understanding how a lemon grove works, not clocking up miles.
299918P1.consiglio: Pick the 5pm slot between May and September: it's cooler under the pergola and from the viewpoint the bay catches the late-afternoon light. If you're coming from Naples, allow more than an hour and a half between the Circumvesuviana train to Sorrento and the SITA bus to Massa Lubrense, so catch an early train. If you're driving, stick to one small glass: the tastings are generous. Bring an empty bag, because you can buy the jams and liqueurs at the farm.

faq.q: How long does it last and where do we meet?
faq.a: About two hours. You meet at the EAV and SITA bus stop in the main square of Massa Lubrense, and that's where you finish. There are two departures a day, at 10am and 5pm, every day of the week. Pick-up from some hotels in the area can be requested when you book.

faq.q: What does the price include?
faq.a: The guided farm visit and all the tastings: lemonade and lemon slices with sugar on arrival, limoncello, cream of limoncello and orange and cinnamon liqueur at the viewpoint, citrus jams and olive oil at the end. Transport to Massa Lubrense isn't included, except pick-up where available. Prices start at €45 per person.

faq.q: Is it suitable for children?
faq.a: Yes. The route is easy, you can do it with a pushchair and there's a children's rate for ages two to fourteen. Bookings must be made by an adult. The liqueurs are for grown-ups, of course, but the lemonade, sugared lemons and jams are for everyone.

faq.q: What language is the tour in, and can I cancel?
faq.a: The guide speaks Italian and English. You can cancel free of charge up to 24 hours before departure with a full refund, and if the weather rules out the visit it's cancelled, with the option to change date or get a refund. You can book up to ten people at a time.

302203.intro: Two and a half hours on foot in the old town with a licensed guide who is also an archaeologist. You start at the Greek walls in Piazza Bellini and finish at the Duomo, by way of Via dei Tribunali, San Domenico, Spaccanapoli, the church of Purgatorio ad Arco, San Gregorio Armeno and the excavations under San Lorenzo Maggiore. The angle is exactly what the title promises: how Neapolis was born, the cults that piled up on top of each other and the legends Neapolitans still tell.
cosaSiFa: You meet in Piazza Bellini, where the remains of the Greek walls poke through, and from there you turn onto Via dei Tribunali. First stop is the church and square of San Domenico Maggiore, then Spaccanapoli with the Nile statue and a coffee break. The guide has headsets so you can hear even in the noisy lanes.

Next is the church of the Anime del Purgatorio ad Arco, with the traditions tied to the cult of the souls in Purgatory, then up Via San Gregorio Armeno, the street of nativity-scene workshops, to the Banksy mural. At the San Lorenzo Maggiore complex you go inside: beneath the basilica lie the Roman remains, with the mosaics of the ancient city.

The last stop is the Cathedral, with the Chapel of the Treasure of San Gennaro. The tour ends on Via Duomo after about two and a half hours. You'll need comfortable shoes and something to cover your shoulders in the churches. There's also a private option, which can be tailored.
302203.perChi: The right tour if you want to understand the old town, not just photograph it, and if you're back in Naples looking for a deeper take. Good for couples, friends or curious teenagers. Two and a half hours on foot through the lanes, with church visits: not suitable for wheelchair users or anyone who can't manage long walks.
302203.consiglio: Do it in the morning, when the lanes are less crowded. Covered shoulders and comfortable shoes. It ends on Via Duomo: from there you can carry on to the Archaeological Museum or down to Forcella, or head back to San Gregorio Armeno at your own pace to buy a nativity figurine.

faq.q: Where does it start and finish?
faq.a: It starts in Piazza Bellini and finishes on Via Duomo, in front of the Cathedral, after about two and a half hours on foot. The route is indicative and may change, but it always covers the old town between Via dei Tribunali and Spaccanapoli.

faq.q: What's included?
faq.a: A licensed guide who specialises in art and archaeology, a small group and headsets so you can follow the explanation better. Food and hotel pick-up aren't included. On request you can book the private version, which can be tailored.

faq.q: What languages is it in and what should I bring?
faq.a: Italian, English, French or Spanish, depending on the language booked. You'll need comfortable shoes and something to cover your shoulders when going into churches. Free cancellation up to 24 hours before, with a full refund.

30791P767.intro: Half a day on foot with a Neapolitan acting as your host, just for your group of up to eight. There's no fixed route: after booking you fill in a short form with your interests and the host gets in touch to build the itinerary, whether that's the Rione Sanità, the markets, hidden courtyards or spots with a view of the bay. You start from your hotel and go on for two to six hours.
cosaSiFa: Before you even set off: after booking you get an online form where you note what interests you, what you've already seen and what you don't want to miss. The local host writes to you personally and suggests a made-to-measure tour: history, food, neighbourhoods or a mix of everything.

On the day, the host picks you up at your hotel and you walk. Depending on what you've chosen, you might go among the stalls of a street market, into the lanes of the Rione Sanità, into the courtyards of old palazzi, to family-run bars or up to one of the spots overlooking the bay.

There's no group of strangers: it's you and the host, so you set the pace, with breaks when you need them. How long it lasts depends on the option booked, from two to six hours, and the content changes from group to group.
30791P767.perChi: For anyone who doesn't want to follow a guide's umbrella and would rather have a tour made for them: families with children of different ages, groups of up to eight friends, people on their second trip to Naples who've already seen the main sights. Makes less sense if you have three hours in total and just want the list of monuments: that's what the classic tours are for.
30791P767.consiglio: Fill in the form carefully, it's what shapes the day: say whether you enjoy walking, whether you have children, whether you've already done the old town. Comfortable shoes either way. If you go for the longer version, ask to take in the Sanità or Posillipo, which are harder to navigate on foot on your own.

faq.q: How does the personalisation work?
faq.a: After booking you receive an online form to note your interests and preferences. The host contacts you personally and builds a made-to-measure itinerary: history, food, neighbourhoods or lesser-known places, based on what you've written.

faq.q: How long does it last and for how many people?
faq.a: From two to six hours, depending on the option chosen. It's a private tour for your group, up to eight people, starting from your hotel.

faq.q: What language is it in, and can I cancel?
faq.a: English and Italian. Free cancellation up to 24 hours before, with a full refund.

308572P2.intro: Two hours inside the Herculaneum ruins with a guide licensed by the Campania Region and a group of no more than fifteen. Herculaneum was buried by the same eruption of AD 79 that covered Pompeii, but here pyroclastic flows buried it under twenty metres of scorching material and preserved it better: it's smaller, it was wealthier, and the original decoration can still be seen in the houses. Explanations in Italian, English or German. The entry ticket is bought separately.
cosaSiFa: You meet at the entrance to the Herculaneum ruins. The guide sets out the difference from Pompeii straight away: same eruption, different effects. Here it was pyroclastic flows, a mass of scorching ash, that swept into the houses, sealed them and hid them twenty metres below the level of the modern town, which now towers above them. They've stayed that way for almost two thousand years.

You then walk through the streets and homes of what was a residential town for wealthy families: you go into the houses to see the original decoration, the floors and details that were lost at Pompeii. The guide chooses the stops based on the group and the areas open that day, and explains why two cities struck by the same disaster have come down to us so differently. Two hours in all, with no more than fifteen people, so you hear everything without headsets.
308572P2.perChi: For anyone who's already seen Pompeii or prefers a more compact site, one you can properly understand in two hours rather than half a day of walking: couples, families with older children, ancient history lovers. The small group helps if you like to ask questions. Less suited to anyone after the scale and crowds of Pompeii, or who doesn't want to pay for the ticket separately.
308572P2.consiglio: Buy your entry ticket before the meeting time, because it isn't included. Hat, water and closed shoes: you're outdoors and walking over stones. Herculaneum is reached from Naples on the Circumvesuviana and is on the way to Vesuvius: ruins in the morning and crater in the afternoon, or the other way round, makes a full but doable day.

faq.q: Is the entry ticket included?
faq.a: No. The price covers the Region-licensed guide for two hours in a group of no more than fifteen; entry to the ruins is bought separately and must be done before the meeting time, so the group can go in on schedule. Explanations are in Italian, English or German.

faq.q: How long does it last and how many people are there?
faq.a: The visit lasts about two hours and the group is limited to fifteen. It's a format designed for understanding the site at an easy pace, going into the houses and asking questions without having to chase after a big tour group. You meet at the Herculaneum ruins.

faq.q: Herculaneum or Pompeii?
faq.a: They're different: Pompeii is huge and needs half a day; Herculaneum is smaller, was wealthier and is better preserved, with the house decoration still easy to read. If you're short on time or have already been to Pompeii, Herculaneum in two hours gives you more. Free cancellation up to 24 hours before.

332811.intro: Two hours in a real pizzeria in the centre to learn Neapolitan dough with four ingredients and fold a calzone properly, into a half-moon. Everyone has their own workstation, the master pizzaiolo teaches staglio, the technique for shaping dough balls, and at the end you eat your own savoury calzone with a glass of wine or beer, followed by a sweet calzone made from the same dough and filled with chocolate cream. Explanations in Italian and English, small groups.
cosaSiFa: You meet in Piazza Bovio and go into the pizzeria. You start with the basics: water, flour, salt and yeast, and how those four ingredients become an elastic dough. The pizzaiolo shows the kneading, explains the rising and teaches staglio, the technique for dividing the dough into round, even balls. Everyone works at their own station.

When the dough is ready you stretch it and fill it with local produce: San Marzano tomatoes, smoked provola, ricotta, Neapolitan salame, basil, extra virgin olive oil and pepper. Then you learn to seal the edges to get the half-moon shape and it goes into the pizzeria's oven, where the calzone bakes in front of everyone.

You sit down at the table and eat your own calzone with a glass of wine, beer or water. You finish with little fried dough bites filled with chocolate cream and a limoncello. You leave with the digital recipe so you can make it all again at home. It lasts about two hours.
332811.perChi: For couples, friends and families with children aged six and over: younger children aren't allowed in the work area or near the oven. Good if you want to take home a technique, not just a dinner, because you genuinely work the dough. Not suitable for anyone gluten intolerant. If you're short on time, it's done in two hours, meal included.
332811.consiglio: Wear clothes that can take some flour and tie your hair back. Don't eat beforehand: savoury calzone, sweet calzone and wine make a full meal. Piazza Bovio is halfway between the port and the old town, so beforehand you can see Piazza Municipio and the Maschio Angioino castle, or afterwards walk up to Spaccanapoli. It often sells out, so book early.

faq.q: What's included in the class?
faq.a: The hands-on class in the pizzeria with your own workstation, a full meal with the savoury and sweet calzone you've made, a glass of wine, beer or water, a limoncello to finish, water, and the digital recipe to take home. You don't need to bring anything.

faq.q: Can children take part?
faq.a: Yes, but only from age six. For safety reasons younger children can't enter the work area or go near the oven, so they can't attend even as spectators. Explanations are in Italian and English.

faq.q: How long does it last and where do we meet?
faq.a: About two hours, including dough, filling, baking and eating. The meeting point is Piazza Bovio, in the centre. There are also options for small groups or private classes. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before, with a full refund.

353209P1.intro: Three hours by boat along the Posillipo coast with a marine biologist and a licensed guide, in a group of no more than ten. You leave from the pier on Via Caracciolo, cruise past caves carved out by the Romans, snorkel with the gear provided (wetsuit included in the colder months) and land on a little beach known almost only to Neapolitans. Beer and taralli (crunchy Neapolitan savoury biscuits) on board, with a deck shower, sun canopy and fridge.
cosaSiFa: You board at the Via Caracciolo pier and, as the boat pulls away from the seafront, the guide tells the story of the city seen from the sea while the biologist explains what lives in these waters. The boat is set up for comfort: deck shower, music, a canopy for shade, fridge and cushions.

Once below the Posillipo hill you pass the Roman-era caves cut into the rock and make the first stop for swimming and snorkelling. Mask and snorkel are provided, plus a wetsuit in the colder months. If you can't swim, you can still get in the water and stay close to the boat.

The next stop is Villa Lauro, where you land on a small, tucked-away beach with a view of the bay. Throughout the trip you're offered drinks and nibbles, beer and taralli. You're back at the starting pier after about three hours.
353209P1.perChi: For anyone who wants to see Naples from the water without the crowds of the big boats: couples, friends, families with children over two. Non-swimmers can still come and get in the water beside the boat. If you get seasick, bring your own medication. Children under two aren't allowed.
353209P1.consiglio: Swimsuit on already, towel, hat and sun cream, and a bag that can get wet. Calm-sea days are best for snorkelling: if the weather turns, the trip can be cancelled up to half an hour before. Before or after, the seafront and Castel dell'Ovo are a short walk from the pier.

faq.q: What's included in the boat trip?
faq.a: The licensed guide, the marine biologist, snorkelling gear with a wetsuit in the colder months, and drinks and nibbles on board, beer and taralli. The boat has a deck shower, canopy, fridge, cushions and music. The group is no more than ten people.

faq.q: Do I need to be able to swim?
faq.a: No. Non-swimmers can get in the water and stay close to the boat. Children under two can't take part. If you get seasick, bring your own medication, as none is provided on board.

faq.q: What language is it in, and how does cancellation work?
faq.a: English, Spanish and Italian. Free cancellation up to 24 hours before. In bad weather the trip can be cancelled up to half an hour before departure. The starting point is the Via Caracciolo pier, on the seafront.

357930.intro: A tour on a fat e-bike, the electric bikes with wide tyres, that does what normal bikes in Naples don't: climb. From the Plebiscito to the seafront, then Mergellina and up to the Sant'Antonio terrace in Posillipo and the Parco Virgiliano, with the bay, Pozzuoli, Ischia and Procida in front of you. You finish at Castel dell'Ovo. Guide, helmet, earpieces, snack and water included, with hotel pick-up.
cosaSiFa: You start with a fifteen-minute briefing on how to use the fat e-bike and a few rules for staying relaxed in traffic. Then you're off: Piazza del Plebiscito and the Royal Palace, then Via Caracciolo with the view of the bay, the shopping street of Via dei Mille and Mergellina, with the Fountain of Partenope.

From Mergellina you climb, and this is where the motor earns its keep: the Sant'Antonio terrace in Posillipo, with the city below, and the Parco Virgiliano, from where you see Pozzuoli, Ischia and Procida. Along the way the guide talks through the earpieces, so you can hear even at the back of the group. There's a break with a snack and water.

The last leg is downhill to Castel dell'Ovo, where the guide tells the legend of the egg. There's also an evening version and a seven-hour one that continues to Pompeii, so the tour lasts two to seven hours depending on the option chosen.
357930.perChi: For anyone who wants the views from up high without doing the climbs on leg power: the e-bike does the work. Good for couples and friends, including teenagers used to cycling. Not suitable for anyone with mobility issues or using a wheelchair. If you're not at ease in traffic, be aware that you ride on open roads, with the guide leading the way.
357930.consiglio: Closed shoes and comfortable clothes, plus a light jacket for the ride down from Posillipo. If you can choose, late afternoon gives the best light from the Virgiliano. Hotel pick-up is included, so there's no need to get to the starting point on your own. Afterwards, the seafront for a stroll on foot.

faq.q: How long is the tour?
faq.a: It depends on the option: from two to seven hours. The basic ride covers the centre, the seafront and the Posillipo hills; there's an evening version and a long seven-hour one that goes as far as Pompeii.

faq.q: What's included?
faq.a: The fat e-bike, the local guide, earpieces to hear them, a helmet with a disposable hygienic liner, a snack, a bottle of water and hotel pick-up and drop-off.

faq.q: What language is it in, and can I cancel?
faq.a: Italian, English, French, Spanish and German. Free cancellation up to 24 hours before, with a full refund. Not recommended for anyone with reduced mobility.

39613P103.intro: Two and a half hours between the Naples above ground and the Naples below. You start in Piazza Bellini, go down into the tunnels and chambers beneath San Lorenzo, where the remains of the Roman city lie, with the market, the public buildings and traces of the forum, then climb back up to walk along Spaccanapoli to San Gregorio Armeno, the street of nativity-scene workshops. Entry to Neapolis Sotterrata and guide included, groups of up to fifteen.
cosaSiFa: Meet in Piazza Bellini. From there the guide leads the group through the streets of the centre, stopping along the way to explain what you're seeing, and takes everyone to the entrance of the excavations beneath San Lorenzo Maggiore, where the underground part begins.

Below ground you walk through passages, tunnels and excavated rooms: the level of the Roman city, with the market square, the public buildings and what's left of the forum. The guide explains how this layer stayed intact beneath a city that kept growing on top of it, century after century.

You come back up into daylight and carry on along Spaccanapoli, the dead-straight street that cuts through the old town, with the everyday life of its shops and lanes. You finish in San Gregorio Armeno, among the stalls of artisans who make nativity scenes all year round.
39613P103.perChi: For first-timers in Naples who want the old town and what lies beneath it in one go. Good for couples, friends and families with older children; groups are no more than fifteen. You walk for two and a half hours, with stairs down and back up: bear that in mind if you have mobility issues.
39613P103.consiglio: Comfortable shoes and a light sweatshirt: underground the temperature drops, even in summer. Mornings are best, when Spaccanapoli is still bearable. You finish in San Gregorio Armeno: from there the Duomo and the Sansevero Chapel are five minutes' walk away, handy for filling the afternoon.

faq.q: What's included?
faq.a: The guide and entry to Neapolis Sotterrata, the archaeological site beneath San Lorenzo. The tour lasts two and a half hours, in groups of up to fifteen.

faq.q: What language is it in?
faq.a: English and Italian, chosen when you book.

faq.q: Where do we meet, and can I cancel?
faq.a: In Piazza Bellini, in the old town. The route ends in San Gregorio Armeno. Free cancellation up to 24 hours before.

39613P228.intro: The royal palace Charles of Bourbon commissioned in 1750 to rival Europe's great courts: 1,200 rooms, designed by Luigi Vanvitelli, with a park that seems to go on forever. With a group of no more than sixteen you skip the queue, climb the Grand Staircase and walk through the Royal Apartments, then the shuttle takes you to the far end of the park, past fountains and the waterfall, to the English Garden. Three hours, and at the end you're free to stay on in the grounds.
cosaSiFa: Meet in Piazza Carlo di Borbone, at the palace's main entrance, ten minutes before your time. With priority tickets you go straight in, and the first hour and a half is spent in the palace: the Grand Staircase, the chapel, the Royal Apartments with frescoes, gilding and Baroque furniture, and the little court theatre, a miniature echo of the San Carlo. Groups over seven use headsets.

The second part is in the park. You board the shuttle bus included in the price and ride up to the top of the gardens, with fountains and sculptures inspired by classical mythology and the waterfall. From there the guide takes you into the English Garden, full of exotic plants and flowers, where the visit ends.

The tour finishes there, in the middle of the English Garden: if you like, you can stay on and explore the gardens on your own, with no need to keep to the group's schedule, perhaps walking back down the avenues and pools towards the palace. Getting back to Caserta or Naples is up to you, as is getting there.
39613P228.perChi: For anyone who wants to see the palace without losing an hour in the queue or wearing themselves out on three kilometres of avenues: the shuttle sorts that. Suitable for all fitness levels, but it isn't wheelchair accessible and isn't recommended for anyone with back problems. Guide dogs are allowed.
39613P228.consiglio: Comfortable shoes, because between the rooms and the gardens you still walk a fair bit. Getting to the meeting point isn't covered by the tour: from Naples the train to Caserta is your best bet, as the station is a short walk from the palace. After the visit, if you have time, stay in the gardens until closing.

faq.q: How long does it last and where do we meet?
faq.a: Three hours: an hour and a half in the palace and an hour and a half in the park. Meet in Piazza Carlo di Borbone, in front of the palace's main entrance, at least ten minutes before the start, with your voucher on your phone or printed.

faq.q: What does the price include?
faq.a: The three-hour guided visit, skip-the-line tickets for the palace, the English Garden ticket, the shuttle to get there and headsets for groups over seven. Tips and transport to the meeting point aren't included.

faq.q: What language is it in, and can I cancel?
faq.a: The tour is available in Italian and English, depending on the date. Cancel at least 24 hours before the scheduled start for a full refund. Groups are no more than sixteen people.

396673.intro: Two hours on foot that bring together the Naples of grand monuments and the Naples of the back lanes. You start near Piazza del Plebiscito, pass the San Carlo opera house and the Galleria Umberto, then climb into the Quartieri Spagnoli (the Spanish Quarter), among street art, washing lines and the stepped lanes that cut up the hill, as far as the Maradona murals. You head down to the Pignasecca market for a taste of street food and finish on Spaccanapoli.
cosaSiFa: The meeting point is at the start of Via Chiaia, in front of a historic café, a stone's throw from Piazza del Plebiscito. The first stretch is monumental Naples: Teatro San Carlo, the Galleria Umberto, and the square with the Royal Palace as a backdrop. With six or more people, headsets are used so you can hear the guide over the traffic.

Then you enter the Quartieri Spagnoli, the most densely packed part of the city: a grid of uphill lanes, steps, laundry on the balconies and the street art that has filled them in recent years. The unmissable stop is the Maradona murals, the most photographed in Naples. From here you head down towards the Pignasecca.

The Pignasecca is a real working market, with food and clothes stalls, and this is where you have the included tasting, sweet or savoury. The tour ends on Spaccanapoli, in front of the Gesù Nuovo church, the Immacolata obelisk and Santa Chiara. It runs in all weather, rain included, with no postponements.
396673.perChi: For first-timers in Naples with an afternoon to spare: in two hours you see the monumental centre, the Quartieri and the market, and get a feel for how the city fits together. Good for couples, families with older children and solo travellers. The Quartieri are all slopes and steps: worth knowing if walking is hard for you.
396673.consiglio: Go in the morning: the Pignasecca is in full swing at that hour and the food is freshly made. Comfortable shoes, there's a lot of up and down. You finish on Spaccanapoli, so keep the time after free for the Veiled Christ or San Gregorio Armeno, a few minutes away. The tour runs with at least four people per language; otherwise it becomes bilingual.

faq.q: Where does it start and how long does it last?
faq.a: The meeting point is in front of a historic café at the start of Via Chiaia, next to Piazza del Plebiscito. The tour lasts two hours and ends on Spaccanapoli, in the old town. It runs in any weather, so bring an umbrella if it's raining.

faq.q: What languages is it available in?
faq.a: Italian, Spanish, French and English, with a live guide. The tour is guaranteed with at least four participants per language: if the minimum isn't reached, it may be run in two languages at once so it can still go ahead. Earpieces are provided for groups of six or more.

faq.q: What's included?
faq.a: The local guide, earpieces from six participants up, and a street food tasting at the Pignasecca, sweet or savoury. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the start, with a full refund. Departure times are shown when you choose a date.

408790.intro: Three hours in the saddle, crossing Naples from one end to the other: from the seafront with Vesuvius ahead to the Decumani, the oldest part of the city. You start near the port, ride along the sea to Castel dell'Ovo and Borgo Marinari, then head up towards Piazza del Plebiscito and Via Toledo and finish in the lanes of the Greek and Roman centre. The guide rides with the group and tells the stories; the bike and water are included, and so are child seats.
cosaSiFa: The meeting point is the rental shop near the port, where you collect your bike; it's worth arriving fifteen minutes early to adjust saddles and child seats. The first stretch is the easiest: the seafront, flat and wide, with Castel dell'Ovo and the Borgo Marinari on one side and Vesuvius on the other. You carry on along Via Caracciolo towards Mergellina and Chiaia, with stops for photos and the guide's explanations.

Then you head into the city: Piazza del Plebiscito with the Royal Palace and the basilica of San Francesco di Paola, then Via Toledo, Piazza Carità and Piazza del Gesù Nuovo. Here the traffic and pedestrians pick up and you ride slowly, in single file behind the guide, who picks the route and stops the group when needed.

The last part is in the Decumani, the street grid laid out by the Greeks: Via dei Tribunali, Via Anticaglia, Spaccanapoli, the Duomo. These are narrow lanes with a church on every corner, and here the bike is mostly for getting from one stop to the next. At the end you ride back to the start and return the bike. The route may change because of traffic or weather.
408790.perChi: Good if you're confident on a bike and not put off by Neapolitan traffic: you ride among scooters and pedestrians, and there are a few climbs. Children can come along in child seats, always with an adult. Not suitable if you have back problems, are pregnant or use a wheelchair. If you'd rather not work too hard, ask for an e-bike, paid separately on the day.
408790.consiglio: In summer pick the morning departure: there's no shade on the seafront and midday is punishing. Closed shoes, sunglasses and sun cream, plus a light backpack for water. If you reach the Decumani around lunchtime, you're a step from Via dei Tribunali and Spaccanapoli for a quick bite on the go.

faq.q: How long is the bike tour and where does it start?
faq.a: About three hours, starting and finishing at the same point near the port, where you collect your bike. The operator asks you to arrive 15 minutes before your booked time. The route is indicative and may be changed, especially because of weather: in bad weather the tour may be moved or cancelled.

faq.q: What's included and what isn't?
faq.a: The guide, the bike, child seats and water are included. Hotel pick-up, food and drinks and tips aren't. E-bikes are available for a supplement, paid directly on the day of the tour.

faq.q: What languages is it in, and can I cancel?
faq.a: The tour runs in Italian, English, Dutch, Spanish, French and German: you choose the language when you book. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before departure, with a full refund. Under-18s must be accompanied by an adult.

415352.intro: Two hours in the National Archaeological Museum with an archaeologist and priority entry. The MANN holds what came out of Pompeii and Herculaneum, frescoes and mosaics sealed for centuries by the eruption of AD 79, and the Farnese collection, with the Farnese Hercules and the Farnese Bull. On your own it's easy to get lost among the rooms; with someone who knows where to look, in two hours you see what matters and understand why. Guide in Italian or English, ticket included.
cosaSiFa: You meet in Piazza Museo, in front of the entrance. You go in through the priority lane and start with the Farnese collection, the classical sculptures gathered by the Farnese family: the gigantic Hercules, the Farnese Bull, Greek gods and Roman emperors lined up along the corridors.

Then you move on to the rooms devoted to the Vesuvian cities: frescoes removed from the houses of Pompeii and Herculaneum, mosaics, objects recovered from beneath the ash. The archaeologist explains how they were found, how they survived and what they tell us about the people who lived there.

Finally you pass through the coins and wall paintings, with time to stop in front of whatever strikes you most. The visit lasts about two hours and ends inside the museum. Suitcases, large bags and pushchairs aren't allowed, and the route isn't suitable for anyone with mobility difficulties.
415352.perChi: For anyone going to Pompeii or Herculaneum, before or after: this is where the pieces you won't see at the sites are kept. For lovers of ancient art who want a serious explanation, not a stroll. Two hours in a museum is long with small children; pushchairs aren't allowed and the route isn't suitable for wheelchairs.
415352.consiglio: The museum is a step from Piazza Bellini and Via dei Tribunali: morning at the MANN, lunch in the old town. There's a reduced rate for EU citizens aged 18 to 25, so check how to apply it when booking. Book choosing your language; the tour often sells out.

faq.q: How long does it last and where do we meet?
faq.a: The visit lasts about 2 hours. The meeting point is Piazza Museo, in front of the National Archaeological Museum, next to the Museo metro stop. You go in with priority entry, skipping the regular ticket-office queue.

faq.q: What's included?
faq.a: The museum ticket, priority entry and the guide, who is an archaeologist. Transport, food and drinks aren't included. Suitcases, large bags, pushchairs and non-folding wheelchairs aren't allowed in.

faq.q: What language is it in, and can I cancel?
faq.a: Slots in Italian and English, chosen when you book. Free cancellation up to 24 hours before the start, with a full refund. It's one of the museum's most booked tours, with over six hundred reviews and a 4.8 rating.

420535P5.intro: An hour and a half by boat along the Naples coast, from the Borgo Marinari to the waters off Posillipo, with no more than nine people on board. You pass beneath Castel dell'Ovo and in front of Palazzo Donn'Anna, the unfinished palace that rises straight out of the sea, while the skipper tells stories of the city and its life on the water. When conditions allow, you stop for a swim: soft drinks and snorkelling masks are included. It's the quickest way to see Naples the way the fishermen saw it.
cosaSiFa: You leave from the Borgo Marinari, the little harbour at the foot of Castel dell'Ovo. As soon as you're out of the harbour the castle is right there, seen from the side you can't see from land, and the boat follows the seafront towards Posillipo. The group is small, no more than nine people, so there's no rush and you can chat with the skipper without jostling for space.

You carry on to Palazzo Donn'Anna, which from the sea you can see in full, its façade dropping straight into the water. In the most sheltered stretch, off Posillipo, the boat stops for swimming and snorkelling: the masks are on board, along with the soft drinks. Throughout the trip the skipper talks about the history of the coast and Neapolitan seafaring culture, with stories about the palazzi and the caves you can only see from here. You're back at the Borgo Marinari after about an hour and a half, with time to dry off before you step ashore.
420535P5.perChi: Designed for couples, families and groups of friends who want a break from the heat and the lanes without going all the way to Capri. Also good if you're short on time, because ninety minutes later you're back on dry land on the seafront. Less suited to anyone who gets seasick or doesn't want to get wet: the swim is the part everyone looks forward to.
420535P5.consiglio: Swimsuit on already, towel and sun cream, because you'll be swimming and there's little shade on the boat. The hour before sunset gives the best light on Vesuvius. Before or after, walk round Castel dell'Ovo and grab something on Via Partenope. On summer weekends, book a few days ahead.

faq.q: How many people are on board?
faq.a: No more than nine. It's a small boat, designed precisely to keep away from the crowded ones: you can hear the skipper without a microphone, switch sides for photos with no trouble, and the swimming stop is more relaxed. Explanations are in Italian or English.

faq.q: What's included and what should I bring?
faq.a: Soft drinks and snorkelling masks are included. Bring a swimsuit, towel, sun cream and a light sweatshirt for the ride back if you go out towards evening. The trip lasts about an hour and a half, starting and finishing at the Borgo Marinari, below Castel dell'Ovo.

faq.q: Can I cancel if the weather is bad?
faq.a: Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before departure, with a full refund. If the sea is too rough to go out, the operator will offer you another time or a refund: either way, it's best not to leave the decision to the last minute.

424784.intro: An hour beneath the Quartieri Spagnoli (the Spanish Quarter), in tunnels Neapolitans dug over centuries: first cisterns and aqueduct channels, then, in the Second World War, shelters from the bombing raids. You go down with a guide, walk through narrow passages and can still see the writing left on the walls by the people who hid there. It's one of the most booked visits in Naples, and the priority-entry ticket is included.
cosaSiFa: You meet in the Quartieri Spagnoli, at the site entrance. The guide gives a short introduction above ground, then you go down. The first tunnels give your eyes time to adjust to the dark and help you understand how the city was shaped from below, starting with the Greeks, who were the first to dig here.

You carry on through the channels of the old aqueduct, with narrow passages and a few steps, and reach the spaces used as air-raid shelters during the war. Here the guide describes what life underground was like during the bombing and shows you the writing still on the walls. After about an hour you head back up, your head full of stories and legends.
424784.perChi: Good if you're short on time: in an hour you see a side of Naples you'd never imagine from street level. Teenagers like it too, because the guide mixes history with storytelling. Avoid it if you're claustrophobic or find walking difficult: there are narrow tunnels and stairs. It isn't wheelchair accessible.
424784.consiglio: It's cooler underground than on the street: a light sweatshirt and closed shoes are all you need. Book a few days ahead, because slots fill up fast. When you come out you're already in the Quartieri Spagnoli: carry on through the lanes on foot or head down to Via Toledo, just round the corner.

faq.q: How long is the visit and where does it start?
faq.a: The visit lasts one hour and starts in the Quartieri Spagnoli, where you meet the guide before going down into the tunnels. The exact meeting point may vary depending on the language booked and is given in your confirmation.

faq.q: Is it suitable for everyone?
faq.a: No. The operator advises against it for anyone who is claustrophobic, has mobility difficulties or uses a wheelchair: the route has narrow tunnels and some stairs. Comfortable shoes are enough; you don't need any other gear.

faq.q: What's included and what languages is it in?
faq.a: The guided tour, entry and the priority ticket that lets you skip the ticket-office queue are included. The visit is in Italian, English or Spanish: you choose the language when you book. Free cancellation up to 24 hours before, with a full refund.

42520.intro: Capri without queuing at the port ticket office: the hydrofoil is already booked, and on the island there's a minibus to take you up to Anacapri and a guide who walks with you. Eight hours in all, with the fifty-minute crossing from Naples, the upper part of the island, Capri town with the Piazzetta, and entry to the Giardini di Augusto, the spot for photographing the Faraglioni rocks. Free time rounds it off, then it's back to Naples.
cosaSiFa: You meet at the port of Naples, with the option to add a pick-up in the city. You board the hydrofoil, fifty minutes across the bay, and land at Marina Grande. There, instead of queuing for public transport, the group gets on a private minibus that climbs the hairpin road up to Anacapri, with the sea below.

In Anacapri you walk round the village with the guide: it's quieter and higher up. Then you head down to Capri town: the Piazzetta, the boutique-lined lanes, stories of the island told along the way. You go into the Giardini di Augusto, terraces above the sea with views of the Faraglioni. The rest of the day is yours: lunch, handmade sandals, a stroll. Then the hydrofoil back.
42520.perChi: For anyone who wants to see Capri in a day without sorting out ferries and minibuses themselves, and for cruise passengers: the day is timed around return schedules. Not suitable for wheelchair users or anyone who finds walking difficult, as the island is all slopes and steps. The Blue Grotto and Monte Solaro aren't included.
42520.consiglio: Comfortable shoes and travel light: no suitcases on board. Lunch isn't included, and during free time in Capri places fill up quickly, so decide in advance where you want to eat. In high season departures are confirmed with at least two people, in low season with four. If you're arriving on a cruise, give your ship and port when booking.

faq.q: Where does it start and how long does it last?
faq.a: From the port of Naples, with an optional paid pick-up in the city. The day lasts about eight hours: fifty minutes by hydrofoil on the way out, the guided visit to Anacapri and Capri, free time and the hydrofoil back. The exact meeting point depends on the option chosen.

faq.q: Who goes with us, and in what language?
faq.a: A licensed local guide, in English, Italian, Spanish or French depending on the date. The tour may be run in two languages on the same day. On the island the group travels by private minibus between Marina Grande, Anacapri and Capri, there and back.

faq.q: What's included and how do I cancel?
faq.a: Return hydrofoil between Naples and Capri, guide, minibus on the island and a ticket for the Giardini di Augusto. Not included: lunch, drinks, tips, the Blue Grotto and the Monte Solaro chairlift. You can cancel free of charge up to 24 hours before and pay later.

436379.intro: Three hours in a kitchen in the old town making, yourself, the two things everyone wants to take home from Naples: a pizza, Margherita or Marinara, and a tiramisù. You work the dough by hand, learn mozzatura, bake in a proper wood-fired oven and at the end sit down to eat what you've made, with wine, beer or a soft drink. Small groups, twelve people at most, and recipes to take away.
cosaSiFa: You start with dessert, so it has time to set. You whip the mascarpone cream, dip the biscuits in coffee and build the tiramisù in layers, with cocoa on top. The chef explains how to tell when the cream is the right consistency and how not to over-soak the biscuits. Meanwhile, bruschetta arrives with local tomatoes and homemade bread.

Then it's the pizza's turn. You mix and work the dough from scratch, learn mozzatura, the art of shaping dough balls by hand, and stretch the base without a rolling pin, just with your fingers. You also make the tomato sauce and top your own Margherita or Marinara. The chef shows off a few tricks with the dough too.

The pizza goes into the wood-fired oven and you watch it puff up and turn golden, while the chef explains how heat and baking time change the result. Then you sit down: you eat your pizza with a glass of wine, beer or a soft drink, finish with the tiramisù and a taste of limoncello. You leave with a diploma and the recipes to make it all again at home.
436379.perChi: Good for couples, families and groups of friends; under-18s must be with a parent or guardian. Vegetarians and vegans need to say so when booking. The three hours are spent standing at the counter, so it's not suitable for anyone who can't stand for long, and it isn't wheelchair accessible. If you're short on time, it doubles as a full meal.
436379.consiglio: Book ahead, places often run out. Arrive hungry: between bruschetta, pizza and tiramisù it's a proper meal, so pick a lunch or dinner slot and don't eat beforehand. Short sleeves and comfortable shoes, flour gets everywhere. Afterwards, Via dei Tribunali and Spaccanapoli are right outside for a stroll.

faq.q: How long is the class and what's included?
faq.a: Three hours. Included are the chef, all ingredients and utensils, apron and hat, the bruschetta to start, the pizza and tiramisù you make, a drink of your choice (wine, beer or soft drink), a taste of limoncello, the diploma and the recipes to take home.

faq.q: What language is the class in?
faq.a: The instructor speaks Italian, English, French and Spanish. You choose the language when you book; that's also when to mention any dietary needs, vegetarian, vegan or otherwise, which are catered for.

faq.q: Can I cancel my booking?
faq.a: Yes, cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the start, with a full refund. You can also book now and pay later. The exact meeting point depends on the option chosen and is given after booking.

436503.intro: Three hours in a kitchen in the old town learning two egg pastas rolled out with a rolling pin, no machine: ravioli and fettuccine, each with its own sauce, plus a tiramisù put together at the start and eaten at the end. You begin with tomato bruschetta on homemade bread and finish at the table with what you've made and a drink. More than twelve hundred reviews averaging 4.9: it's the highest-rated pasta class we list.
cosaSiFa: You start backwards, with dessert. The tiramisù is assembled first, with mascarpone, savoiardi (ladyfingers) dipped in coffee and cocoa, then goes in the fridge to set while you work on the rest. Meanwhile you nibble on bruschetta with local tomatoes, put on your apron and chef's hat, and get the organic eggs, flour and rolling pin ready.

The long part is the dough: mixing, kneading, resting, then rolling the sheet out by hand, keeping an eye on pressure and thickness, the way it was done in every home before pasta machines. Fettuccine and ravioli come out of that sheet. Meanwhile you make the two sauces: butter and Parmigiano for the fettuccine, San Marzano tomato and basil for the ravioli.

At the end everyone sits down together and eats what came out, with an alcoholic or soft drink of your choice and unlimited water. The tiramisù comes last, properly chilled by now. Before you leave you get the recipes, a pasta-maker diploma with your name on it and an instant photo.
436503.perChi: Good for couples, families and solo travellers: you work side by side and the group loosens up quickly. You don't need to know how to cook. Under-18s must come with an adult. Vegetarians and vegans need to say so when booking. It isn't accessible to wheelchair users, and with three hours on your feet it's best to arrive rested.
436503.consiglio: Book it as lunch or dinner and don't eat beforehand: between bruschetta, two pastas and tiramisù you'll leave full. The exact meeting point depends on the option chosen and comes with your confirmation, but it's in the old town: Spaccanapoli and San Gregorio Armeno pair nicely before or after. Comfortable clothes, without wide sleeves that end up in the flour.

faq.q: What language is the class in?
faq.a: The instructor speaks Italian, English, French and Spanish. You choose your language when you book. The class lasts three hours and includes everything: ingredients, professional equipment, apron and hat, the opening bruschetta, a drink and the meal of what you've made.

faq.q: What do we eat at the end?
faq.a: The fettuccine with butter and Parmigiano sauce, the ravioli with San Marzano tomato and basil, the opening bruschetta and the tiramisù you made at the start of the class. With unlimited water and a drink of your choice, alcoholic or not. It counts as a full lunch or dinner.

faq.q: Can I cancel? And what about children?
faq.a: Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before. Under-18s are welcome but must be accompanied by a parent or guardian; they can't attend alone. If you follow a vegetarian, vegan or special diet, say so when booking so the kitchen can plan for it.

437021.intro: A two-hour walk through the lanes of the Quartieri Spagnoli (the Spanish Quarter), led by someone who knows them, to read the murals by Cyop & Kaf, Bosoletti, Mandragora and Juan Pablo Gimenez and see how street art has changed the face of the neighbourhood. You pass the Maradona mural and dozens of lesser-known works, with stories of everyday life. If you like, you can add an hour underground, in the cisterns and shelters of Napoli Sotterranea.
cosaSiFa: You start in Piazzetta Matilde Serao, just off Via Toledo, with a ten-minute introduction. Then you enter the Quartieri from Via Sant'Anna di Palazzo and walk for about twenty minutes past the first murals, while the guide explains how an area with a bad reputation became a creative workshop.

The heart of the tour is inside the Quartieri, in stretches of ten to twenty-five minutes, among large and small works, legends and anecdotes about life in the lanes. The stop at the Maradona mural lasts ten minutes, with a short break right after. The walking part ends on Via Toledo.

If you've chosen the option, you carry on with a guided hour in Napoli Sotterranea (underground Naples), priority entry included: tunnels, cisterns of the old aqueduct and chambers carved into the tuff rock, also used as shelters in the Second World War. This part costs extra and is available only in Italian and English, so if you book in Spanish or French you can't add it.
437021.perChi: For anyone who wants to see the Quartieri Spagnoli with someone who can explain them, for street art fans and for football fans on a Maradona pilgrimage. 94 per cent of Italian participants gave it full marks. Less suited to anyone who doesn't enjoy walking uphill through narrow, crowded lanes.
437021.consiglio: Comfortable shoes and sunglasses: the lanes are steep and the tour runs in any weather. If the underground interests you, take the option straight away: it costs more but saves you a second outing. Be on time, because there's no refund if you're late.

faq.q: How long does it last?
faq.a: The walk through the Quartieri Spagnoli lasts about two hours. With the Napoli Sotterranea option you add a guided hour, for about three hours in total. The walking part ends on Via Toledo.

faq.q: What languages is it available in?
faq.a: The walk runs in Italian, English, Spanish or French depending on the date booked. The Napoli Sotterranea option, however, is available only in Italian and English, so bear that in mind when choosing.

faq.q: What's included, and can I cancel?
faq.a: The guide, the walking tour and printed material. If you choose the option, the priority ticket for Napoli Sotterranea too. Transport isn't included. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before, with a full refund.

437675.intro: You ride the Centrale funicular up to the Vomero and walk back down to the Quartieri Spagnoli (the Spanish Quarter), by way of Via Palizzi and the Petraio steps. In two hours you see Naples from above, with the bay, Capri and Vesuvius in front of you, then plunge into the lanes, the murals and the Pignasecca market. The guide speaks Italian, English, French or Spanish, and the funicular ticket is included. One of the loveliest walks in the city, and the funicular does the climbing.
cosaSiFa: You meet near the Augusteo station of the Centrale funicular and ride up to the Vomero in ten minutes, a hilltop district of Art Nouveau buildings and tree-lined streets. From Via Palizzi the view opens over the bay, with Capri, Vesuvius and the coast on the horizon: the guide stops here to talk about the city and you take the first photos. It's the quietest and most scenic part of the tour.

Then you start down the Petraio steps, the path linking upper and lower Naples, with one long stretch of about 35 minutes' walking and other short stops for photos. You cross Corso Vittorio Emanuele, and with every step the neighbourhood changes: from the quiet buildings of the Vomero to the washing lines and voices of the lanes.

The last part, about 25 minutes, is inside the Quartieri Spagnoli, among the alleys and murals. The tour ends on Via Pignasecca, at the market, among fish stalls and street food. The funicular is one way only: the return is all downhill, on foot, over steps and paving stones.
437675.perChi: Suits people who enjoy walking and want to get a grip on Naples in two hours, as a couple, with friends or with teenagers. It's almost all downhill, but on long, uneven flights of steps: not recommended for anyone with heart problems, who isn't fit, or who uses a wheelchair. Pushchairs aren't allowed. If you want an effortless outing, this isn't it.
437675.consiglio: Comfortable shoes with good grip, because the Petraio steps are worn smooth. Bring water in summer. Lateness at the meeting point isn't refunded, so arrive ten minutes early. You finish at the Pignasecca: the perfect moment for a cuoppo (a paper cone of fried food) or a pizza a portafoglio (a pizza folded in four to eat on the go).

faq.q: What languages does the tour run in?
faq.a: The guide is available in Italian, English, French and Spanish: you choose the language when you book. There's also a private option if you want the group to yourselves. The meeting point may change depending on the option chosen, so check your confirmation.

faq.q: Is the funicular included? What about getting back?
faq.a: Yes, the one-way ticket on the Centrale funicular up to the Vomero is included. You don't need a return, because you walk down the Petraio steps to the Quartieri Spagnoli and the Pignasecca, which are already in the centre.

faq.q: How much walking is there really?
faq.a: About an hour and a half of walking out of two hours in total, almost all downhill, with stops for photos and explanations. The steps are long and the surface is uneven: bear that in mind if you have dodgy knees. People with mobility difficulties can't take part.

439400.intro: Two hours inside the Pignasecca, the city's oldest open-air market, with six tastings running from savoury to sweet: you start with a spritz and a board of mozzarella and cured meats, move on to a warm tarallo, pizza a portafoglio, a meatball in ragù and a cuoppo of fried fish, and finish with babà, sfogliatella or gelato alongside a limoncello or a coffee. You start from Piazza Carità, and the guide speaks Italian, English, French or Spanish. You'll leave full.
cosaSiFa: The meeting point is Piazza Carità, in front of the church of San Liborio, and within fifteen minutes you're in Piazza Pignasecca. You open with the welcome spritz and a board of mozzarella and local cured meats. Then it's off to a historic bakery in the market for a Neapolitan tarallo (a savoury ring studded with almonds and pepper) still warm, and on through the stalls for pizza folded in four.

The fourth stop is the polpetta, a meatball cooked in ragù; the fifth is the cuoppo, a paper cone of mixed fried fish, eaten standing up the way it's done here. Each stop lasts about fifteen minutes, with short walks between stalls while the guide tells stories and legends behind the dishes. Six stops in all, in two hours.

You finish with a dessert of your choice, babà, sfogliatella or artisan gelato, with a limoncello or an espresso, just outside the market. There's a vegetarian version of the tour and a private option if you want the group to yourselves. If you have allergies or restrictions, say so in advance.
439400.perChi: For anyone short on time who wants the best of Neapolitan street food in one lunch: couples, friends, solo travellers. It also works for vegetarians and vegans if they say so when booking, because there's a dedicated version. Less suited to anyone who doesn't like eating on their feet in a busy market or can't face fried food.
439400.consiglio: Book the morning slot: the market is at its liveliest before lunch and the fish stalls are full. Comfortable shoes and an empty stomach: six tastings are not a snack. The Pignasecca is a step from Via Toledo and the Toledo metro station: afterwards, walk up into the Quartieri Spagnoli.

faq.q: What languages is the tour available in?
faq.a: Italian, English, French and Spanish. There's also a private option and a version with vegetarian food. The meeting point may change depending on the option chosen, so check your booking confirmation carefully before you head out.

faq.q: What do the six tastings include?
faq.a: A welcome spritz with a board of mozzarella and cured meats, a Neapolitan tarallo, folded pizza, a meatball in ragù, a cuoppo of mixed fried fish and a traditional dessert or gelato with limoncello or espresso. Extra drinks and tips aren't included.

faq.q: How long does it last, and can I cancel?
faq.a: About two hours, from Piazza Carità through the Pignasecca market. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the start, with a full refund, and you can book now and pay later. The price may vary depending on the date and the number of participants.

458455.intro: Three hours by boat along the Naples coast at the hour when the sun drops behind Posillipo. You leave from the pier on Via Caracciolo, pass beneath Castel dell'Ovo and cruise past the Posillipo villas to the tuff quarries of Trentaremi bay, which can only be seen from the sea. At some point the boat stops: spritz, tomato bruschetta and fried bites, music, and a dip for anyone who wants one. You're back at the pier after dark. Rated 4.7 from over three hundred reviews.
cosaSiFa: You meet at the pier on Via Caracciolo, on the seafront, where the boat is waiting. You set off in the late afternoon and head straight for Castel dell'Ovo, then along the Via Caracciolo waterfront and the Posillipo hill. Your host tells the story of the city from the sea: the history of the clifftop villas, Villa Rosebery, the myths of the bay.

Once at Trentaremi bay, in front of the old tuff quarries, the boat stops. Time for a swim, with snorkelling masks on board for anyone who wants them, and then the aperitivo: a spritz or a soft drink, bruschetta with fresh tomato and Neapolitan fried snacks, with music on board.

The ride back coincides with the actual sunset: the city lights come on as you head back to the pier. You can book a shared small-group version or a private one if you're with a group. The length may vary with the weather, and the commentary on board may be in two languages at once.
458455.perChi: The right choice for couples and groups of friends who want an evening on the water without chartering a whole boat. Fine with teenagers too, if accompanied by an adult. Not suitable if you get seasick, have mobility difficulties or use a wheelchair. If you don't want to get wet, you can stay on board during the stop.
458455.consiglio: Swimsuit under your clothes, towel, hat and sun cream: the late-afternoon sun on the water still bites. Bring a sweatshirt for the way back, when the breeze cools things down. In high season places go fast, so book a few days ahead. Before boarding, a walk along the seafront to Castel dell'Ovo works up an appetite.

faq.q: Where does it leave from and how long does it last?
faq.a: You leave from and return to the pier on the Via Caracciolo seafront in Naples. The trip lasts about 3 hours, sunset included, but may run a little longer or shorter depending on sea and wind conditions.

faq.q: What's included, and can I swim?
faq.a: The skipper, the trip, a spritz or soft drink, the tasting on board with tomato bruschetta and local fried snacks, music and safety equipment are included. There's a swimming stop, with snorkelling kit available. Tips aren't included.

faq.q: What languages is it in, and how does cancellation work?
faq.a: The commentary on board is in English, Italian, Spanish or French, and may be given in two languages on the same trip. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before departure, with a full refund.

458957.intro: Two and a half hours of tastings through the Decumani, in English, starting at the Greek walls in Piazza Bellini and finishing in Piazza del Gesù. You eat in neighbourhood spots and on the street: taralli, frittatina (a deep-fried pasta patty), pizza fritta, mozzarella, babà and gelato, with a spritz and a taste of limoncello along the way. Between stops you pass through Via dei Tribunali, San Gregorio Armeno and Spaccanapoli, so you see the old town while you eat. Portions are generous: by the end it's dinner.
cosaSiFa: The meeting point is Piazza Bellini, next to the remains of the Greek walls, where the guide waits with a sign. After a ten-minute introduction you head to the first stop, a twenty-minute tasting at a local place, then on to Via dei Tribunali for the second, also twenty minutes. Next comes a stop for drinks, ten minutes for a spritz or a limoncello.

You cross Piazza San Gaetano for another tasting, fifteen minutes, and head down Via San Gregorio Armeno to Piazzetta Nilo, where the first dessert arrives. From there you turn onto Spaccanapoli as far as Piazza San Domenico Maggiore for the second dessert. Along the way you also pass through a neighbourhood market for mozzarella and freshly made pizza fritta.

You finish in Piazza del Gesù, in front of the church, after a stretch on Via Toledo. About ten stops in all, half eating and half walking, with the guide telling you about the recipes and the history of the places between bites.
